questions.title: Gradle vs Maven
questions.question: What are the key differences between Gradle and Maven, and when should you choose each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Maven: XML, convention over configuration, opinionated lifecycle, mature ecosystem
- Gradle: Groovy/Kotlin DSL, highly flexible, incremental builds, build cache
- Performance: Gradle's incremental builds and build cache dramatically faster for large projects
- Gradle Daemon: keeps JVM warm — much faster repeated builds
- Dependency management: both use Maven Central; Gradle supports BOM imports too
- Android: Gradle is the only choice
- Spring Boot: supports both; Spring Initializr generates either
- Team familiarity often drives the choice — both are excellent

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Maven and Gradle both handle dependency management, compilation, testing, and packaging, but they take fundamentally different approaches. Maven uses XML and a fixed lifecycle — you configure plugins to hook into predefined phases. This makes Maven predictable and easy to understand, but rigid when you need to do something unconventional.

Gradle uses a Groovy or Kotlin DSL and is far more flexible — build logic is actual code, not configuration. This makes complex builds easier to express, and makes it straightforward to add custom tasks. The other major advantage is performance: Gradle tracks which inputs and outputs have changed and only rebuilds what's necessary. Its build cache can even reuse outputs from other machines, which makes a huge difference in CI for large projects.

For a new Spring Boot microservice, either works well. I'd choose Gradle if the project is complex with many custom build steps, if it's part of a large multi-project build where incremental compilation matters, or if the team already knows Gradle. I'd choose Maven if the team is primarily Java-focused with strong Maven familiarity and you want maximum ecosystem compatibility and tooling support.

speakable_v2.hook: Maven and Gradle both handle dependency management, compilation, testing, and packaging, but they take fundamentally different approaches.
speakable_v2.cap: I'd choose Maven if the team is primarily Java-focused with strong Maven familiarity and you want maximum ecosystem compatibility and tooling support.

questions.title: Gradle Multi-Project Builds
questions.question: How do you structure and optimize Gradle multi-project builds for a Java monorepo?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- settings.gradle: declares all subprojects in the build
- Root build.gradle: shared configuration via allprojects/subprojects
- Convention plugins: extract shared build logic into buildSrc or included build
- Dependency between projects: project(':common') declaration
- Build cache: share cached outputs between CI runs and developers
- Parallel builds: --parallel flag or org.gradle.parallel=true
- Task avoidance: tasks are lazy by default in Gradle 5+ — registered but not configured until needed
- Configuration cache: cache task configuration phase (experimental but very fast)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Gradle multi-project builds are defined in settings.gradle.kts, which lists all subprojects. Shared configuration goes in the root build.gradle.kts using subprojects or allprojects blocks. But the modern recommended approach is convention plugins — reusable build logic packaged in buildSrc that subprojects apply like a regular plugin. This is much cleaner than a large root build script.

Parallel builds are one of Gradle's biggest advantages for multi-project repos. With gradle.parallel=true and the build cache enabled, Gradle identifies which projects are independent and builds them concurrently. The build cache also means if a module's inputs haven't changed since the last CI run, Gradle just restores the cached output instead of rebuilding — this makes CI builds dramatically faster in large repos.

The configuration cache is another significant performance improvement. Gradle normally re-evaluates all your build scripts on every invocation to compute the task graph. The configuration cache saves that computed graph and reuses it when inputs haven't changed, eliminating the configuration phase entirely on subsequent runs.

questions.title: Gradle Dependency Management and Version Catalogs
questions.question: How do you manage dependencies and versions centrally in Gradle using version catalogs?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Version catalog (Gradle 7.4+): centralized version management in libs.versions.toml
- Replaces hardcoded versions scattered across build files
- Type-safe accessors: libs.spring.boot.web instead of string dependency notation
- Bundles: group related dependencies — libs.bundles.testing includes all test deps
- BOM import: platform() function — imports Spring Boot BOM
- Dependency constraints: force specific version across transitive deps
- resolution strategies: force(), substitute(): handle dependency conflicts
- dependencyUpdates plugin: check for newer versions

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Version catalogs, introduced in Gradle 7.4, centralize all dependency versions in a single TOML file called libs.versions.toml. Instead of hardcoding versions in multiple build.gradle files across a multi-project build, you define them once in the catalog and reference them by name using type-safe accessors generated by Gradle.

This is Gradle's answer to Maven's BOM concept. You define versions at the top, map them to library aliases, and optionally group related libraries into bundles. Build files then use libs.spring.boot.web instead of org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web:3.2.5 — cleaner, centralized, and type-safe.

For importing Maven BOMs like Spring Boot's dependency management, Gradle provides the platform() function. This brings in the BOM's dependency constraints, aligning transitive dependency versions the same way Maven's BOM import does.

questions.title: Gradle Testing Configuration
questions.question: How do you configure unit tests and integration tests separately in Gradle?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- test task: default unit test task — runs src/test/java
- Source sets: create integrationTest source set for separate classpath and config
- withType<Test>: configure all test tasks consistently
- useJUnitPlatform(): enable JUnit 5; required in Gradle
- finalizedBy jacoco: generate coverage report after tests
- testLogging: configure what's logged during test run
- Integration test task: separate task that runs after unit tests in CI
- Parallel test execution: maxParallelForks for faster test suite

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Gradle separates tests through source sets and test tasks. The default test task runs unit tests from src/test/java. For integration tests, you create a separate integrationTest source set with its own classpath and a separate test task. This way, developers can run unit tests quickly and integration tests only when needed or in CI.

In CI, the typical pipeline runs unit tests in the test task, and if they pass, runs integration tests in the integrationTest task. The tasks are chained with check depending on both, ensuring both must pass for the build to succeed.

Parallel test execution is an often-overlooked optimization. Setting maxParallelForks to a fraction of available processors can dramatically reduce test suite runtime for large test suites, as long as tests are properly isolated — no shared state, proper test isolation with Testcontainers.

questions.title: Custom Gradle Tasks and Build Automation
questions.question: How do you write custom Gradle tasks to automate build processes?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- tasks.register: define new task — lazy (not configured until needed)
- doFirst/doLast: add actions before or after task execution
- dependsOn: task dependencies — ensures prerequisite tasks run first
- Inputs/outputs: declare task inputs and outputs for up-to-date checks and caching
- Exec task type: run external commands from Gradle
- Copy task type: copy files as part of build
- Task groups and descriptions: organize and document tasks
- buildSrc: reusable custom task types across multi-project

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Gradle tasks are the basic unit of work. Custom tasks extend the build by automating steps that aren't covered by plugins — building Docker images, generating configuration files, running database migrations, or deploying to environments. Tasks are code, so you can use any Groovy or Kotlin logic.

Task inputs and outputs are the key to performance. When you declare a task's inputs and outputs, Gradle can check whether the task is up-to-date — if inputs haven't changed since the last run and outputs still exist, the task is skipped. This is how the build cache works: it stores task outputs indexed by the hash of inputs, so the task result can be reused across machines.

For complex custom build logic that you want to share across modules in a multi-project build, put it in buildSrc. This directory is compiled before the main build and its contents are automatically available as Gradle API in all build files.

questions.title: Gradle Wrapper and Version Management
questions.question: What is the Gradle Wrapper and why is it important for team consistency?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Gradle Wrapper: shell script that downloads and uses a specific Gradle version
- gradlew (Linux/Mac) and gradlew.bat (Windows) — commit to repo
- gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties: specifies distributionUrl (exact Gradle version)
- Benefit: all developers and CI use exactly the same Gradle version — consistent builds
- No Gradle installation required: gradlew downloads the right version automatically
- Update wrapper: ./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.7
- gradle-wrapper.jar: bootstrap code for wrapper — commit to repo

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The Gradle Wrapper is a thin script committed to your repository that downloads and runs a specific version of Gradle. Instead of requiring everyone to install the same Gradle version manually, developers just run ./gradlew. The wrapper checks if the specified version is already downloaded, fetches it if not, and executes it.

This solves the 'it works on my machine' problem for the build tool itself. Without the wrapper, different team members or CI servers might use different Gradle versions, leading to subtle differences in build behavior — different handling of task ordering, different resolution of dependency conflicts, different compiler flags. With the wrapper, everyone uses exactly the same version.

The wrapper configuration is three files: gradlew (Unix script), gradlew.bat (Windows script), and gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties which specifies the exact Gradle distribution URL. All three should be committed to git. The gradle-wrapper.jar bootstrap file is also committed and should be the only binary in your repository.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Wrapper Properties

```properties
# gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties
distributionBase=GRADLE_USER_HOME
distributionPath=wrapper/dists
distributionUrl=https\://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-8.7-bin.zip
networkTimeout=10000
validateDistributionUrl=true
zipStoreBase=GRADLE_USER_HOME
zipStorePath=wrapper/dists
```

## Commands

```bash
# Use wrapper (recommended always)
./gradlew build          # downloads Gradle 8.7 if not present, then builds
./gradlew --version      # verify Gradle version

# Update wrapper to new Gradle version
./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.8
git add gradle/wrapper/
git commit -m "chore: upgrade Gradle to 8.8"

# Verify wrapper integrity (check SHA-256 of downloaded distribution)
./gradlew wrapper --distribution-type bin --gradle-version 8.8 \
  --gradle-distribution-sha256-sum 03fcba7b1ef8d8c34...abc123
# Adding sha256 prevents MITM attacks on the Gradle download
```

## What to Commit

```
✅ Commit:
  gradlew                                 ← Unix/Mac script
  gradlew.bat                             ← Windows script
  gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar       ← bootstrap jar (~55KB)
  gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties← version config

❌ Don't commit:
  .gradle/                  ← build cache (gitignore)
  build/                    ← build outputs (gitignore)
  ~/.gradle/wrapper/dists/  ← downloaded distributions (local)
```

speakable_v2.hook: The Gradle Wrapper is a thin script committed to your repository that downloads and runs a specific version of Gradle.
speakable_v2.cap: The gradle-wrapper.jar bootstrap file is also committed and should be the only binary in your repository.
